Streeter-Phelps marched along **one line** downstream. Air pollution downwind of a stack spreads **across** the wind as well as along it --- a genuinely spatial problem. ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # Point Sources and Receptors ## Some Approaches for Modeling Air Pollution **So far**: box (airshed) models --- overall mass balance across a whole region. **Today**: point sources and receptors --- *plume* models, which track concentration as a continuous function of position. ## Point Sources and Receptors ![Point Source/Receptor Schematic](figures/air-pollution.png){width=75%} ## Emissions Follow Instantaneous Paths ![Point Source Flow Traces](figures/air-pollution-instant.png){width=75%} ## Plume: Time-Averaged Positions ![Point Source Average Plume](figures/air-pollution-plume-timeavg.png){width=75%} ## "Gaussian Plume" ![Gaussian Plume](figures/air-pollution-plume-shape.png){width=75%} ## "Gaussian Plume" ![Gaussian Plume Distribution](figures/air-pollution-plume-dist.png){width=75%} # Deriving the Model ## The Advective-Diffusion Equation The mass balance of a small air parcel: $$\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} - \underbrace{[D+K]\nabla^2 C}_{\text{diffusion}} + \underbrace{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{\nabla}C}_{\text{advection}} = 0$$ - $D$: molecular diffusion coefficient - $K$: dispersion coefficient (turbulent mixing) ::: {.fragment .fade-in} This is the **same equation family** as the airshed and DO models --- just with the spatial term kept instead of dropped or reduced to one line. ::: ## Diffusive Flux :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} ![Diffusive Flux](figures/diffusion-flux.png) ::: ::: {.column width=50%} Concentration gradient + diffusion $\Rightarrow$ flux. **Fick's law**: $$F_x = D\frac{dC}{dx}$$ ::: :::: ## Turbulent Flux :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} ![Turbulent Flux](figures/turbulent-flux.png) ::: ::: {.column width=50%} Concentration gradient + turbulent mixing $\Rightarrow$ flux. $$F_x = K_{xx}\frac{dC}{dx}$$ $K_{xx}$ depends on flow/eddy characteristics --- not a material property like $D$. ::: :::: ## Assumption 1: Steady State $$\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} + \vec{u}\cdot\vec\nabla C - [D+K]\nabla^2C = 0$$ $$\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = 0$$ ## Assumption 2: Wind Only Along $x$ $$\vec{u}\cdot\vec\nabla C = u_x\frac{\partial C}{\partial x} + \cancel{u_y\frac{\partial C}{\partial y}} + \cancel{u_z\frac{\partial C}{\partial z}}$$ ## Assumption 3: Turbulence Dominates Molecular Diffusion, and Along-Wind Dispersion Is Negligible $$-[\cancel{D}+K]\nabla^2C = \cancel{K_{xx}}\frac{\partial^2C}{\partial x^2} + K_{yy}\frac{\partial^2C}{\partial y^2} + K_{zz}\frac{\partial^2C}{\partial z^2}$$ ::: {.fragment .fade-in} This isn't an arbitrary simplification --- it's a **Péclet number** argument, exactly like the one from Week 6: $Pe = uL/D_x \gg 1$ for atmospheric transport at any distance you'd care about. ::: {#cell-fig-peclet .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} u_wind, Dx = 2.5, 50.0 Lvals = 100:50:10000 Pe = u_wind .* Lvals ./ Dx plot(Lvals ./ 1000, Pe, xlabel="Distance [km]", ylabel=L"Pe = uL/D_x", color=cb_vermillion, linewidth=4, legend=false, yscale=:log10) hline!([1], color=:black, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2) plot!(size=(950, 400), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm) ``` ::: {#fig-peclet .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Péclet number for along-wind transport, u = 2.5 m/s, Dx = 50 m²/s. ::: ::: ::: ## What's Left With these three assumptions: $$\bbox[5pt, border: 3px solid red]{u\frac{\partial C}{\partial x} = K_{yy}\frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial y^2} + K_{zz}\frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial z^2}}$$ ::: {.fragment .fade-in} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=70%} Plus a boundary condition: mass flowing through any downwind cross-section must equal the emission rate $Q$: $$Q = \iint u\,C\,dy\,dz$$ ::: ::: {.column width=30%} ![Boundary Condition for the A-D Equation](figures/boundary-mass.png) ::: :::: ::: ## Solving the PDE $$C(x,y,z) = \frac{Q}{4\pi x\sqrt{K_{yy}K_{zz}}}\exp\left[-\frac{u}{4x}\left(\frac{y^2}{K_{yy}} + \frac{(z-H)^2}{K_{zz}}\right)\right]$$ ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Substitute $\sigma_y^2 = 2K_{yy}\dfrac{x}{u}$, $\sigma_z^2 = 2K_{zz}\dfrac{x}{u}$ --- the distance a diffusing parcel has spread by the time it reaches $x$: ::: ## The Gaussian Plume $$C(x,y,z) = \frac{Q}{2\pi u\sigma_y\sigma_z}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{y^2}{\sigma_y^2} + \frac{(z-H)^2}{\sigma_z^2}\right)\right]$$ A Gaussian distribution in $y$ and in $z$ --- which is where the name comes from, and why $\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ read exactly like standard deviations. # The Ground Is a Boundary Condition ## Reflection ![Reflected Mass Off Ground](figures/reflection.png){width=65%} Pollutant doesn't vanish into the ground: $\partial C/\partial z = 0$ at $z=0$ --- a **Neumann** condition. ## Enforcing It With an Image Source :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=30%} Add a second, "reflected" source below ground, the mirror image of the real one. ::: ::: {.column width=40%} ![Reflected Mass Off Ground](figures/reflection-image.png) ::: :::: ## Final Model: Elevated Source With Reflection $$C(x,y,z) = \frac{Q}{2\pi u\sigma_y\sigma_z}\exp\left(\frac{-y^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right)\left[\exp\left(\frac{-(z-H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) + \exp\left(\frac{-(z+H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right)\right]$$ ## Does the Image Term Actually Work? ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} plume_params = let Q, H, u_wind = 100.0, 41.0, 2.5 (; Q, H, u_wind) end sig_y(xk) = 34.0 * xk^0.894 function sig_z(xk) if xk < 1 return 14.35 * xk^0.740 - 0.35 else return 62.6 * xk^0.180 - 48.6 end end function plume(xk, y, z, params; reflect=true) sy, sz = sig_y(xk), sig_z(xk) base = (params.Q / (2π * params.u_wind * sy * sz)) * exp(-y^2 / (2sy^2)) real_source = exp(-(z - params.H)^2 / (2sz^2)) if reflect image_source = exp(-(z + params.H)^2 / (2sz^2)) else image_source = 0.0 end return base * (real_source + image_source) end dz = 0.001 flux_with = (plume(3.0, 0.0, dz, plume_params) - plume(3.0, 0.0, 0.0, plume_params)) / dz flux_without = (plume(3.0, 0.0, dz, plume_params; reflect=false) - plume(3.0, 0.0, 0.0, plume_params; reflect=false)) / dz ``` ::: $\partial C/\partial z$ at the ground, 3 km downwind: **with** the image term, 1\.3e\-9; **without** it, 4\.5e\-5 --- about $3\times 10^4$ times larger. The second exponential is not decoration; it is the boundary condition. ## Final Model Assumptions 1. Steady-state 2. Constant wind velocity and direction 3. Wind $\gg$ dispersion in the $x$-direction 4. No reactions 5. Smooth ground (no extra turbulent eddies or reflections) # Dispersion and Atmospheric Stability ## Estimating Dispersion "Spread" $\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ matter enormously for the plume's footprint. What sets them? **Main driver**: atmospheric stability --- greater stability means less vertical/cross-wind spreading. Pasquill (1961): six stability classes. ## Atmospheric Stability Classes | Class | Stability | Description | |:----:|:----------|:-----------| | A | Extremely unstable | Sunny summer day | | B | Moderately unstable | Sunny & warm | | C | Slightly unstable | Partly cloudy day | | D | Neutral | Cloudy day or night | | E | Slightly stable | Partly cloudy night | | F | Moderately stable | Clear night | ::: {.caption} Source: ::: ## Estimating Dispersion "Spread" $$\sigma_y = ax^{0.894}, \qquad \sigma_z = cx^d + f$$ ![Dispersion Coefficients](figures/plume-dispersion.png) ::: {.caption} Source: ::: **Note**: here $x$ is in km, while $y,z$ in the plume equation are in m. # Worked Example ## Example The emission rate of SO$_2$ from a smokestack is 100 g/s. At **3 km downwind** on a clear fall evening (class F), **what is the centerline ground-level concentration of SO$_2$**? Effective plume height is 41 m; wind speed at that height is 2.5 m/s. $$\sigma_y = 34x^{0.894} \qquad \sigma_z = \begin{cases}14.35x^{0.740}-0.35 & x<1\text{ km} \\ 62.6x^{0.180}-48.6 & x>1\text{ km}\end{cases}$$ ## Working It Through ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} xk = 3.0 sy, sz = sig_y(xk), sig_z(xk) Cground = plume(xk, 0.0, 0.0, plume_params) println("σ_y = ", round(sy, digits=1), " m") println("σ_z = ", round(sz, digits=1), " m") println("C(3 km, 0, 0) = ", round(Cground * 1e6, digits=1), " µg/m³") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` σ_y = 90.8 m σ_z = 27.7 m C(3 km, 0, 0) = 1692.2 µg/m³ ``` ::: ::: - Centerline, ground level: $y=0,\ z=0$ - $\sigma_y \approx$ 91\.0 m, $\sigma_z \approx$ 28\.0 m - $C \approx$ 1692\.0 µg/m$^3$ # Key Takeaways ## Key Takeaways ::: {.incremental} - The plume equation is the same advective-diffusion family as the airshed and DO models --- here the spatial structure is kept rather than simplified away. - Dropping along-wind dispersion is a **Péclet number** argument: $Pe \gg 1$ for atmospheric transport at any distance of interest. - The ground is a **Neumann boundary condition**, enforced with an image source --- verified numerically to kill the vertical flux at $z=0$. - $\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ are empirical, tied to atmospheric stability class --- not derived from first principles. ::: # Upcoming Schedule ## Next Classes **Monday**: Where the plume actually lands --- the footprint on the ground, a vertical section that makes the reflection visible, and what happens when several stacks share an airshed. **Wednesday**: Model validation. How we decide whether to believe any of this. ## Assessments **Homework 4**: Assigned today, due Thursday, October 8. **Mini-Project 1**: Also due Thursday, October 8. # References ## References
